title: Where are you going? — on foot or by transport
title_target: Куда ты идёшь? — Kuda ty idyosh?
goal: Say where you're headed, and face two things at once: Russian has different verbs for going on foot and going by vehicle, and the same preposition changes meaning depending on the noun's ending.
bekal: tell где (where) and куда (where to) apart

dialogs.title: Диалог — On the wrong metro
dialogs.intro: Ani gets lost in a metro station and asks a woman for help. Watch the switch between где and куда — and how the noun endings switch with them.

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: Excuse me, do you know where Red Square is?
lines.literal: excuse-me, you — not — know, where — Red — square?

lines.speaker: Женщина:
lines.id: Red Square? You need Okhotny Ryad station.
lines.literal: Red — square? to-you — needed — station — Okhotny — Ryad.

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: And where is this train going?

lines.speaker: Женщина:
lines.id: This one goes the other way. You need the other platform.
lines.literal: this — rides — in — other — side. to-you — needed — to — that — platform.

lines.speaker: Женщина:
lines.literal: three. then — go — on-foot, five — minutes.

lines.speaker: Женщина:
lines.id: No, I'm going home. I live in the south.
lines.literal: no, I — ride — homeward. I — live — in — south.

lines.speaker: Женщина:
lines.id: Don't mention it. Your Russian is good.
lines.literal: not — for — what. you — well — speak — in-Russian.

notes: **Russian separates going on foot from going by vehicle.** ⚠️ English uses one word, "go," for both, so this choice is genuinely new. **идти** = moving on your own feet. **ехать** = moving by any vehicle — bus, car, train, bike, horse. Using идти for a trip to another city sounds like you're walking hundreds of kilometers.

**Rule of thumb: nearby in town, use идти; out of town or by vehicle, use ехать.** *Я иду в магазин* (I'm going to the store, on foot). *Я еду в Москву* (I'm going to Moscow, by vehicle). If you're unsure in town, ask yourself: are my feet carrying me?

**Где asks "where (at)," куда asks "where to" — and the noun endings differ too.** ⚠️ This is the biggest trap in this unit. Compare: *Я **в** Москв**е*** (I'm **in** Moscow, prepositional -е) with *Я еду **в** Москв**у*** (I'm going **to** Moscow, accusative -у). The preposition is exactly the same. **Only the noun ending** makes the difference, and the meaning changes from staying to moving.

**The preposition still follows the в/на pairs from Unit 10.** If a place uses *на* for "at" (на работе), it also uses *на* for "to" (на работу). If it uses *в* (в магазине), then *в магазин*. So you don't need a second list — just change the ending.

**Домой is a pleasant exception.** "Home(ward)" isn't *в дом* but **домой**, one word with no preposition — just like English "go home," not "go to home." It pairs with **дома** (at home) from Unit 10. *Я еду домой* — I'm going home.
**Пешком means "on foot."** *Идите пешком* — just walk. It's often added even when the verb is already идти, for emphasis.
**Не за что** (*nye za shto*) is the reply to thanks, literally "not for anything" — like "don't mention it." Warmer than пожалуйста and very Russian.

grammars.title: Идти and ехать
body: Two of the most common verbs in everyday Russian, and both are irregular.
after: ⚠️ The past tense is irregular too: идти → **шёл** (m), **шла** (f), **шли** (pl). Ехать → **ехал, ехала, ехали** (regular). The past tense is covered fully in Unit 14.
Идти is also used for things that move without feet: *Поезд идёт* (the train is running), *Дождь идёт* (it's raining), *Фильм идёт* (the film is showing). So it doesn't always mean human feet.

grammars.title: Где vs. Куда — one table that covers it all
body: Different question, different ending, different meaning. Same preposition.
after: Notice that masculine nouns (университет, магазин, центр) **don't change** in the right-hand column — just like the accusative of inanimate nouns in Unit 8. So half of all direction sentences come free.

⚠️ The question must match too. *Где ты?* is answered with *В университете*. *Куда ты?* is answered with *В университет*. Answering with the wrong ending is one of the mistakes native speakers notice fastest.

blocks.text: To say how you travel, use **на + prepositional** — the same form as "at." The logic: you're *on* the vehicle.

blocks.title: Ready-made phrases for getting around
items: **Как доехать до …?** (*kak da-YE-khat' da*) — How do I get to …? The standard way to ask directions by transport. After до use the genitive: *до центра*, *до вокзала*.
**Как пройти до …?** — How do I walk to …? The on-foot version.
**Мне надо выходить?** (*mnye NA-da vy-kha-DEET'*) — Do I need to get off?

**Вы выходите?** — Are you getting off? ⚠️ An essential phrase on the packed Moscow metro: before the doors open, people ask this of whoever is standing in front of them. Pushing past without asking is considered rude.
**Я заблудился / Я заблудилась** — I'm lost (m / f).

exercises.prompt: Choose идти or ехать in the correct form.
Change to the form used after в or на for direction (куда).
Put the words in the right order.

items: I'm going to the store. (on foot)
We're going to Moscow by train.
How do I get to the city center?
